SCIENCE_DLP.materials: Object cards, a plastic dropper, water, an empty tray and child-growth cards.
activities: Show two objects and ask which visible property could group them.
Describe a property that can be checked.
Model one sorting rule, safe dropper use over a tray, and ordering baby and child pictures.
Sort cards using one rule, move water in drops and describe a change as a child grows.
Give a new set of four cards. Check the stated rule and four placements, safe transfer of water, and one valid growth change.
Sort and label the groups, show a safe transfer and explain one change such as becoming taller.
Ask where the dropper should be placed after use.
Point to the tray and leave it ready for the next pupil.
SCIENCE_DLP.follow_up: Repeat the sorting or apparatus step with pupils who missed it.

SCIENCE_DLP.materials: Bean growth cards, chick and hen pictures, and individual picture strips.
activities: Show a shoot and a mature plant. Ask what might come before the shoot.
Suggest a seed and explain the clue.
Mix bean growth cards and display a chick and a hen. Ask pairs to discuss visible features before sharing.
Order seed, sprouting seed, seedling and mature plant, then compare the two animals.
Provide a fresh set of shuffled growth cards and duckling and duck pictures. Check the order and one observable similarity or difference.
Order the four stages and say one comparison such as the duckling is smaller than the adult duck.
Ask how to tell a seedling from a sprouting seed.
Point to the young plant's leaves.
SCIENCE_DLP.follow_up: Use matching picture pairs for pupils who need help comparing stages.

SCIENCE_DLP.materials: Torch, screen, opaque card, a low-voltage cell and bulb, leads, sieve, sand and pebbles.
activities: Show a shadow and ask how the torch, card and screen are placed.
Point to the card between the torch and screen.
Set up a shadow, a circuit with one loose lead and a sand–pebble mixture. Model one check at each station.
Move the card, close the circuit and select a sieve because the grains and pebbles differ in size.
Observe each pupil at the stations or ask for a marked diagram. Check that the card blocks light, the gap is closed, and a sieve traps pebbles.
Explain the shadow, reconnect the loose lead and select a separation tool with a reason.
Ask what happens when the circuit is opened again.
Predict that the bulb goes out and explain that the path is broken.
SCIENCE_DLP.follow_up: Revisit the station corresponding to each pupil's incorrect explanation.

SCIENCE_DLP.materials: Water-cycle pictures, a paper sailboat, a fan, trays and a simple model with illustrated instructions.
activities: Show a paper sailboat and ask what can move it without touching the hull.
Suggest moving air and point to the sail.
Model labelling water vapour and clouds. Demonstrate the sailboat with the fan on and off, then compare a model with its drawing.
Arrange cycle cards, compare the boat's motion and match pieces to the assembly drawing.
Give a fresh diagram and a model with one piece missing. Check the cycle order, the wind explanation and the missing piece using the instructions.
Label water, vapour, clouds and rain in order. Explain that moving air pushes the sail and point to the missing piece.
Ask which stage sends water back towards rivers and seas.
Point to rain and describe where it flows.
SCIENCE_DLP.follow_up: Match symbols to steps again with pupils who missed a cycle label or model part.

MATH_DLP.materials: Base-ten blocks, place-value mats and digit cards.
activities: Show 407 and ask which digit tells how many tens it has.
Point to zero and describe its place.
Build 304 and 460. Compare the role of zero on both mats and write expanded forms.
Place hundreds, tens and ones, then write 300 + 0 + 4 and 400 + 60 + 0.
Give 508 and 750 to each pupil. Check two partitions and the value named for all six digits.
Build and partition both numbers, then state each digit's value including zero.
Swap the 5 and 8 in 508 and ask what changes.
Name the new number and explain the changed values.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Rebuild numbers with an empty tens column before giving a new example.

MATH_DLP.materials: Number cards, a 0–1,000 number line, trays of counters and answer slips.
activities: Show 296 and 310 and ask which is closer to 300.
Use distances of 4 and 10 to explain the choice.
Model estimating a tray using a group of ten as a benchmark. Use a number line to compare and round amounts.
Estimate the number of counters and explain how repeated groups of ten helped.
Check ascending order for 482, 257, 635 and 683 and rounds 300, 500, 600 and 700 in that order. Check one justified counter estimate.
Order and round the four cards, then record an estimate with a reason based on a benchmark.
Ask why 635 and 683 round to different hundreds.
Locate 650 between the two numbers.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Mark the midpoint again for pupils who rounded to the wrong hundred.

MATH_DLP.materials: Base-ten blocks, place-value mats and addition cards.
activities: Show nine ones and three ones. Ask how to record twelve ones.
Exchange ten ones for one ten and retain two ones.
Model 267 + 158 = 425 with exchanges in the ones and tens columns. Let pairs check by subtracting 158 from 425.
Explain both exchanges and use blocks or subtraction to check the sum.
Check 348 + 176 = 524 and 135 + 248 + 107 = 490. Look for a valid model or inverse check.
Solve both on a place-value mat or in columns and show a check for each sum.
Ask why a carried ten belongs in the tens column.
State that ten ones have the same value as one ten.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Rebuild the column in which the exchange was missed.

MATH_DLP.materials: Place-value mats, base-ten blocks and one incorrect worked example.
activities: Display 402 and ask what zero tells us about the tens.
Explain that the number has no tens before regrouping.
Model exchanging one hundred into ten tens and one of those tens into ten ones. Compare this with crossing out zero without an exchange.
Build 402, then explain why 3 hundreds, 9 tens and 12 ones keep its value.
Give the incorrect statement 503 − 278 = 335. Check the corrected answer 225 and both exchanges.
Correct the calculation independently and explain how 503 was rewritten without changing its value.
Ask how addition can check the answer.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Use blocks to trace the exchange that a pupil omitted.

MATH_DLP.materials: Square counters, grid boards and multiplication cards.
activities: Show three rows of four counters. Ask how many in each row.
Say four in each of three rows and count twelve.
Build 6 × 7 and 7 × 8. Split an array into familiar groups of five and the remaining rows.
Use a split such as five sevens and one seven, then join the partial products.
Give 6 × 8 and 7 × 9. Check both arrays and products 48 and 63.
Build or sketch the two arrays, label rows and columns and write each product.
Rotate an array and ask which dimensions change.
Explain that the number of counters stays the same.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Practise one missed fact by rebuilding it in two smaller arrays.

MATH_DLP.materials: Counters, sorting cups, group mats and answer cards.
activities: Show fourteen counters and groups of four. Ask what remains after making full groups.
Make three groups and identify two left over.
Model 53 ÷ 10 as five groups with three remaining. Check with 5 × 10 + 3 and compare the remainder with the divisor.
Make equal groups and write the matching multiplication and addition.
Check 29 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 1 and 46 ÷ 10 = 4 remainder 6. Check both inverse equations and the size of each remainder.
Share or group the counters, record both results and verify them.
Ask why a remainder of four cannot be left when making groups of four.
Explain that those counters make another complete group.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Use a group mat to check that no full group remains uncounted.

MATH_DLP.materials: Situation cards, operation symbols and answer slips.
activities: Tell a short story about gaining seven pencils. Ask what happens to the total.
Explain that it increases and suggest addition.
Contrast combining, comparing, equal groups and equal sharing. Let pairs invent a story for 4 × 6.
Match each story to a symbol and explain what its numbers count.
Use 23 and 17 joined, 23 compared with 17, four bags of six, and 24 shared equally among four. Check +, −, ×, ÷ and one correct answer with a reason.
Match all four stories, solve one and write why the operation fits.
Ask what singles out the equal-sharing story.
Identify a total split into equal groups.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Ask pupils who chose the wrong operation to act out the situation with counters.

MATH_DLP.materials: Equal-length strips, coloured pencils, rulers and answer slips.
activities: Hold up two strips of different lengths. Ask if one half of each strip is the same length.
Identify that the wholes differ.
Use equal strips to model one half and three quarters. Line up the start points to compare the shaded parts.
Fold or partition each strip equally, shade and compare.
Give equal strips for 2/5 and 3/5. Check equal partitions, shading and the conclusion 2/5 < 3/5.
Shade both fractions and explain why the full strips must have equal length.
Ask what the denominator tells us.
State the number of equal parts in the whole.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Guide pupils to align the whole strips before shading a new pair.

MATH_DLP.materials: Blank 0–1 number lines, tenths grids and number cards.
activities: Show one shaded square in a ten-square strip. Ask for two names for its value.
Say one tenth and zero point one.
Place 3/10 and 0.3 on one line. Compare 0.3 and 0.6 by counting ticks from zero.
Match decimal and fraction cards and explain the shared position.
Give 2/10, 0.2, 7/10 and 0.5. Check both cards at 0.2, one at 0.7, and 0.5 between them.
Plot the four cards and explain why 2/10 and 0.2 coincide.
Ask which representation means five of ten equal parts.
Point to 0.5 and give the fraction 5/10.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Use a ten-cell strip for pupils who misread the first decimal place.

MATH_DLP.materials: Play money, blank receipts and price cards.
activities: Show prices RM2.40 and RM1.35. Ask how to line up the amounts.
Match ringgit with ringgit and sen with sen.
Model a receipt for RM3.20 and RM2.45. Count up from RM5.65 to RM10.00 to check RM4.35 change.
Add prices by place value and use coins to count up to the amount paid.
Give a new receipt with RM2.40 and RM3.35 paid with RM10.00. Check total RM5.75, change RM4.25 and an addition check.
Calculate both values and show that the total and change make RM10.00.
Ask why sen values use two digits.
Say that 100 sen make one ringgit.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Practise the exchange between ringgit and sen when needed.

MATH_DLP.materials: Budget cards, price labels and play money.
activities: Give a budget of RM8 and a price of RM6. Ask how much remains.
Identify RM2 as the amount remaining.
Model saving first from a RM12 budget. Let pairs choose items within the amount left.
Make a shopping choice, calculate remaining money and explain what can be saved.
Give RM15.00 with a notebook RM7.50, pencil RM2.30 and ruler RM4.20. Check a choice of exactly two items, its total and remaining savings.
Choose two items, show the addition and subtract the total from RM15.00.
Ask how choosing a less expensive item affects savings.
Explain the amount left increases by the price difference.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Distinguish total spent from savings with a two-column record.

MATH_DLP.materials: Mini clocks, five-minute tick cards and activity slips.
activities: Move the minute hand one large mark. Ask how many minutes passed.
Count five minutes.
Show 8:20 and 8:45. Mark five-minute jumps and compare a count-up method with subtraction.
Set both clocks and count five jumps for 25 minutes.
Give reading at 9:15 and art at 9:50. Check correct hands, written times and the interval of 35 minutes.
Set or draw both times independently and show the seven five-minute jumps.
Ask where the hour hand points at 9:50.
Identify a point between 9 and 10, nearer 10.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Match hand positions to a written time before repeating the interval question.

MATH_DLP.materials: Centimetre rulers, scales, erasers, books and recording sheets.
activities: Show an eraser and a book. Ask which likely weighs more and how to check.
Make a prediction and suggest the scale.
Demonstrate zero alignment for length and taring the scale for mass. Let pairs choose cm and g for the objects.
Estimate both lengths and masses, then measure and compare with estimates.
Give each pupil two objects and check the two estimated and measured lengths and masses. Accept values matching the available instruments.
Enter every result with cm or g and state one estimate that was above or below the reading.
Ask why a mass written without a unit cannot be checked.
Say that the value must identify the measurement unit.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Reteach the specific zero mark or scale reading that was missed.

MATH_DLP.materials: Measuring jugs, water trays, and 150 mL, 500 mL and 2 L container cards.
activities: Show a spoon and a large water jug. Ask which unit suits each.
Suggest mL for the spoon and L for the jug.
Compare the container capacities and read a jug at eye level. Ask pairs to show two measures of 150 mL.
Read the marks and combine the amounts to get 300 mL.
Check sensible units for 150 mL cup, 500 mL bottle and 2 L jug, a 200 mL reading, and 200 + 300 = 500 mL.
Choose units, measure 200 mL and solve how much water the two pours make.
Ask why two pours must use the same unit before adding.
Explain that the values must count the same sized units.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Match capacities to labelled containers before repeating the practical reading.

MATH_DLP.materials: Card nets, cube model, tape and sketch slips.
activities: Show a cube and ask what shape an unfolded face makes.
Identify a square.
Compare a working cube net of six connected squares with six squares in a straight row. Fold the valid arrangement and explain overlap in the other.
Predict, test and point to where the straight row overlaps.
Offer a cross made from four squares in a row with one above and one below the second square, and the straight row. Check choice and six square faces.
Select the cross, identify all six faces and write or say why the straight row fails.
Ask whether six squares alone guarantee a cube net.
Explain that their arrangement must allow all faces to close without overlap.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Fold the incorrect net again to find the overlapping faces.

MATH_DLP.materials: Plane-shape cards, grid paper and a circle stencil.
activities: Show a square and a triangle. Ask what can be counted along the edges.
Identify straight sides and vertices.
Model sorting cards by number of straight sides and vertices. Compare a square with a non-square rectangle.
Sort and label triangles, circles and four-sided shapes and justify one placement.
Give a triangle, square, non-square rectangle and circle. Check sorting and two labelled sketches with correct side and vertex counts.
Classify all four cards, draw two shapes and explain both placements using their properties.
Ask which two shapes share four straight sides but can have different adjacent side lengths.
Name the square and the non-square rectangle.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Trace the corners and sides one at a time with pupils who mixed the counts.

MATH_DLP.materials: Matching horizontal and vertical bar charts, rulers and answer slips.
activities: Show one vertical and one horizontal bar. Ask what must be checked before reading a count.
Point to the numbered scale.
Give two charts of the same votes with bars for drawing, reading and puzzles. Trace vertical bar tops and horizontal bar ends to their scales.
Read one category on both charts and explain why the readings agree.
Use scale marks at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 for counts 8, 6 and 4. Check all three counts from each chart and difference of 4 between drawing and puzzles.
Record each count from both charts and calculate the requested difference.
Ask if the first bar must have the largest value.
Explain that the scale reading determines the largest value.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Practise tracing bar ends on a scale marked in twos.

MATH_DLP.materials: Survey chart, two shop price cards and play money.
activities: Show a bookshop survey. Ask which category has the most votes and how to tell.
Name the longest bar and read its value from the scale.
Use one sample to show how chart counts answer demand and how a price comparison answers cost.
Point to the evidence used for each kind of answer.
Use survey counts of six notebooks, four pencils and two rulers. A notebook costs RM4.60 at A and RM4.30 at B. Check most votes, RM0.30 difference and RM5.70 change from RM10 at B.
Read the chart, select the cheaper shop and show the subtraction for difference and change.
Ask how to verify the change.
Add RM4.30 and RM5.70 to get RM10.00.
MATH_DLP.follow_up: Reteach chart or money work based on the calculation each pupil missed.
